intro: The 13 questions below follow the style of DeepMind's early "quizzes": each question is short and answered out loud, with any formulas you need written on paper, and the answers are definite. Every question states all the conditions it needs, so each can be done on its own; wherever numbers appear, work out the numbers.
solutionIntro:
This round tests the fundamentals of an undergraduate reinforcement learning course: whether you can state definitions precisely, whether you remember the conditions of the theorems, and whether you can get a small set of numbers right on the spot. The interview reports only say that the quiz included reinforcement learning, without recording specific questions; the questions on this page were written to that level of difficulty. Reinforcement learning for LLM post-training (policy gradients, PPO, GRPO, DPO) is on a separate page, RL for LLMs, and is not repeated here.

Three things to prepare. First, drill the Bellman equations, the three TD targets, the UCB index and the importance weight until you can write them from memory. Second, pair every result with a small example of two or three states and work it through by hand; the most common thing an interviewer does is give you a few numbers and have you compute on the spot. Third, state theorems with their conditions: tabular or with function approximation, whether the data come from the current policy, what the step sizes must satisfy, whether rewards are bounded. Most follow-up questions land on the conditions.

questions.q: A two-state Markov decision process (MDP) with discount factor γ=0.8. State A: action stay gives reward +1 and stays in A; action go gives reward −1, moves to B with probability 3/4, and stays in A with probability 1/4. State B: action stay gives reward +5, stays in B with probability 3/4, and returns to A with probability 1/4; action cash gives reward +7 and always returns to A. Policy π chooses go in A and cash in B. Write down the Bellman expectation equations satisfied by Vπ(A) and Vπ(B), solve for the two values, and explain why the solution is unique.
questions.a:
For policy π, the value equals "the reward at this step, plus the discounted expected value of the next state":

Vπ(A)=−1+0.8[41​Vπ(A)+43​Vπ(B)],Vπ(B)=7+0.8Vπ(A).

The first equation rearranges to 0.8Vπ(A)=−1+0.6Vπ(B). Substituting the second: 0.8Vπ(A)=−1+4.2+0.48Vπ(A), i.e. 0.32Vπ(A)=3.2. So

Vπ(A)=10,Vπ(B)=7+0.8×10=15.

Why the solution is unique: write the equations in matrix form V=rπ​+γPπ​V, i.e. (I−γPπ​)V=rπ​. Each row of Pπ​ is a probability distribution, so all its eigenvalues have modulus at most 1; hence the eigenvalues of γPπ​ have modulus at most γ<1, and I−γPπ​ is invertible. Another way to say it: the operator TπV=rπ​+γPπ​V is a γ-contraction in the infinity norm, so its fixed point is unique.

The conditions used are γ<1 and bounded rewards. If γ=1, the task has to be episodic and this policy has to reach a terminal state with certainty; otherwise the value may be undefined.

questions.q: A two-state MDP with discount factor γ=0.8. State A: stay gives +1 and stays in A; go gives −1, moves to B with probability 3/4, and stays in A with probability 1/4. State B: stay gives +5, stays in B with probability 3/4, and returns to A with probability 1/4; cash gives +7 and always returns to A. The value of policy π (go in A, cash in B) has already been computed: Vπ(A)=10, Vπ(B)=15. (a) Compute the four action values Qπ(s,a) and do one step of policy improvement to get a new policy π′. (b) Find Vπ′. (c) Use the Bellman optimality equation to decide whether π′ is an optimal policy. (d) If at every step you only pick the action with the largest immediate reward (stay in A, cash in B), what is the value?
questions.a:
(a) The action value is defined as Qπ(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)Vπ(s′). Plugging in Vπ=(10,15):

  • Qπ(A,stay)=1+0.8×10=9;
  • Qπ(A,go)=−1+0.8(0.25×10+0.75×15)=−1+0.8×13.75=10;
  • Qπ(B,stay)=5+0.8(0.75×15+0.25×10)=5+0.8×13.75=16;
  • Qπ(B,cash)=7+0.8×10=15.

In each state take the action with the largest Qπ: A still chooses go (10>9), and B switches to stay (16>15). So π′ is "go in A, stay in B".

(b) Set up the equations for π′: V(A)=−1+0.8[0.25V(A)+0.75V(B)], V(B)=5+0.8[0.75V(B)+0.25V(A)]. The second simplifies to 0.4V(B)=5+0.2V(A), i.e. V(B)=12.5+0.5V(A); the first is 0.8V(A)=−1+0.6V(B). Substituting gives 0.8V(A)=6.5+0.3V(A), so Vπ′(A)=13, Vπ′(B)=19. Both states are higher than the original (10,15).

(c) Recompute the backed-up values of the four actions with Vπ′=(13,19): in A, stay is 1+0.8×13=11.4 and go is −1+0.8(0.25×13+0.75×19)=13; in B, stay is 5+0.8×17.5=19 and cash is 7+0.8×13=17.4. The maximum in each state is exactly 13 and 19, i.e. Vπ′ itself, so Vπ′ satisfies the Bellman optimality equation V(s)=maxa​[r(s,a)+γ∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)V(s′)]. This equation has a single solution when γ<1, so Vπ′=V∗ and π′ is optimal. Policy iteration finishes in one step here.

(d) Choosing stay in A means staying in A forever: V(A)=1/(1−0.8)=5, V(B)=7+0.8×5=11. It takes the largest available reward at every step, yet in the long run gets well under half of the optimal values (13,19): go loses 1 right now, but what it buys is entry into state B, worth +5 per step.

What is used here is the policy improvement theorem. Conditions: finitely many states and actions, γ<1, and Qπ exact. Conclusion: the π′ obtained by acting greedily with respect to Qπ is no worse than π in every state; if no state strictly improves, π already satisfies the optimality equation. When Qπ is only approximate, this guarantee no longer holds.

questions.q: Suppose the MDP has bounded rewards, ∣r(s,a)∣≤Rmax​, and discount factor γ<1. The Bellman optimality operator is defined as (TV)(s)=maxa​[r(s,a)+γ∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)V(s′)]. (a) Prove that T is a γ-contraction in the infinity norm: ∥TV−TU∥∞​≤γ∥V−U∥∞​. (b) Use this to explain why value iteration Vk+1​=TVk​ converges, and give an upper bound on ∥Vk​−V∗∥∞​. (c) Take γ=0.8, Rmax​=7, V0​=0: according to this bound, how many iterations guarantee an error of at most 0.01? (d) A concrete example: a two-state MDP with γ=0.8; state A: stay gives +1 and stays in A; go gives −1, moves to B with probability 3/4, and stays in A with probability 1/4; state B: stay gives +5, stays in B with probability 3/4, and returns to A with probability 1/4; cash gives +7 and always returns to A. Its optimal values are V∗(A)=13, V∗(B)=19. Starting from V0​=0, compute V1​, V2​, V3​ by hand and see how much the error shrinks each iteration; how many iterations are actually needed before the error is at most 0.01?
questions.a:
(a) First prove a small fact: for any two sets of numbers f(a), g(a), ∣maxa​f(a)−maxa​g(a)∣≤maxa​∣f(a)−g(a)∣. Let a⋆ maximize f; then maxf−maxg≤f(a⋆)−g(a⋆)≤maxa​∣f(a)−g(a)∣; swapping f and g gives the other direction.

For any V, U and state s, let f(a)=r(s,a)+γ∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)V(s′), and let g(a) be the same expression with V replaced by U. Then

∣(TV)(s)−(TU)(s)∣≤amax​ γ​s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)(V(s′)−U(s′))​≤γ∥V−U∥∞​.

The last step uses that p(⋅∣s,a) is a probability distribution: the absolute value of a weighted average is at most the largest absolute value. Taking the maximum over s gives ∥TV−TU∥∞​≤γ∥V−U∥∞​.

(b) Bounded functions with the infinity norm form a complete space, and when γ<1, T is a contraction mapping. By the Banach fixed-point theorem, T has a unique fixed point, which is V∗; and starting from any bounded V0​,

∥Vk​−V∗∥∞​≤γk∥V0​−V∗∥∞​.

The conditions are γ<1 and bounded rewards (so that ∥V∗∥∞​≤Rmax​/(1−γ)). Note two things: the contraction is with respect to the infinity norm and does not necessarily hold for the 2-norm; and if you follow T with a function approximation step (a projection), the combination is not necessarily a contraction either, which is exactly where the divergence in Q12 comes from.

(c) With V0​=0, ∥V0​−V∗∥∞​≤7/(1−0.8)=35. We need 35×0.8k≤0.01, i.e. k≥ln3500/ln1.25=8.161/0.2231=36.57, so 37 iterations. In general k≥ln(Rmax​/((1−γ)ϵ))/ln(1/γ), roughly 1−γ1​ln(1−γ)ϵRmax​​: the number of iterations is proportional to 1/(1−γ). For the same accuracy, γ=0.99 needs 1111 iterations.

(d) Iteration by iteration (in each state, take the max over the two actions):

  • V1​=(max(1,−1), max(5,7))=(1,7);
  • V2​: in A, stay is 1+0.8×1=1.8 and go is −1+0.8(0.25×1+0.75×7)=3.4; in B, stay is 5+0.8(0.75×7+0.25×1)=9.4 and cash is 7+0.8×1=7.8. So V2​=(3.4,9.4);
  • V3​: in A, go is −1+0.8(0.25×3.4+0.75×9.4)=5.32; in B, stay is 5+0.8×7.9=11.32; both exceed the other action (3.72 and 9.72). So V3​=(5.32,11.32).

The distances to V∗=(13,19) are 19 (V0​), 12, 9.6, 7.68. After the first iteration, each iteration multiplies the error by exactly 0.8. The reason is that V1​=V∗−12⋅1: both components are off by the same amount; and for any constant c, T(V−c1)=TV−γc1 (every backed-up value drops by γc). So Vk​=V∗−12×0.8k−11. We need 12×0.8k−1≤0.01, i.e. k−1≥ln1200/ln1.25=31.77, so in practice 33 iterations are needed.

The bound's 37 iterations is conservative for two reasons: it estimates the initial distance as 35 (it is actually 19; with 19 the bound gives 34 iterations); and the first iteration actually shrinks the error by a factor of 12/19≈0.63, faster than 0.8. In practice you don't know V∗, and the usual stopping rule uses the change between consecutive iterations: ∥Vk+1​−V∗∥∞​≤1−γγ​∥Vk+1​−Vk​∥∞​.

questions.q: Discount factor γ=0.99. A common saying is "the effective horizon is about 1/(1−γ)=100 steps". (a) Give two interpretations that make this statement precise. (b) What fraction of the total discount weight ∑t≥0​γt do the rewards of the first 100 steps account for? (c) How many steps do you need to look at to cover 99% of the weight? (d) When every per-step reward is in [0,1], what is the range of the discounted return? If the trajectory is truncated at step 1000, at most how much of the return is missed?
questions.a:
(a) Two interpretations.

  • Total weight: ∑t≥0​γt=1/(1−γ)=100. When every per-step reward is 1, the discounted return is exactly 100, as if you counted 100 steps without discounting.
  • Random termination: view discounting as "after each step, stop with probability 1−γ". The probability of not having stopped by step t (counting from 0) is γt, so the expected discounted return equals the expected undiscounted return of this randomly terminated process; the total number of steps is geometrically distributed with mean 1/(1−γ)=100 steps.

(b) The share of weight in the first 100 steps is ∑t=099​γt/∑t≥0​γt=1−γ100=1−0.366=0.634. This is close to 1−1/e, because 0.99100≈e−1. In other words, about 37% of the weight lies beyond "100 steps"; the effective horizon is not a cutoff.

(c) We need 1−γn≥0.99, i.e. γn≤0.01, n≥ln100/ln(1/0.99)=4.605/0.01005=458.2, so 459 steps, about 4.6 times the effective horizon.

(d) The return lies in [0, 1/(1−γ)]=[0,100]. Truncating at step H loses at most ∑t≥H​γt=γH/(1−γ); for H=1000 that is 100×0.991000≈0.0043.

questions.q: A tabular control problem with discount factor γ=0.8 and step size α=0.5. The agent acts ε-greedily with ε=0.2: with probability 1−ε it picks the action with the largest current Q value, and with probability ε it picks one of the two actions uniformly at random. The current Q table is Q(A,stay)=6, Q(A,go)=8, Q(B,stay)=12, Q(B,cash)=10. The agent executes go in A, receives reward −1, and arrives in B; the next step happens to be exploration, and it picks cash in B. (a) Write down the update targets of SARSA, Q-learning and Expected SARSA, and compute the updated Q(A,go) for each. (b) In which single term do the three differ? (c) If ε stays fixed at 0.2, what do Q-learning and SARSA each converge to? What conditions does each need?
questions.a:
(a) All three methods update Q(A,go)←Q(A,go)+α[target−Q(A,go)], with targets:

  • SARSA: uses the action actually chosen at the next step. Target =r+γQ(B,cash)=−1+0.8×10=7; after the update, 8+0.5×(7−8)=7.5.
  • Q-learning: uses the maximum at the next state, regardless of what was actually chosen. Target =r+γmaxa​Q(B,a)=−1+0.8×12=8.6; after the update, 8+0.5×0.6=8.3.
  • Expected SARSA: takes the expectation over the next action under the policy. In B the greedy action is stay (12>10), chosen with probability 1−ε+ε/2=0.9, and cash with 0.1; the expected value is 0.9×12+0.1×10=11.8. Target =−1+0.8×11.8=8.44; after the update, 8+0.5×0.44=8.22.

(b) They differ only in the bootstrapping term, i.e. what stands in for "the value after the next state": SARSA uses the sampled Q(s′,a′), Q-learning uses maxa′​Q(s′,a′), and Expected SARSA uses ∑a′​π(a′∣s′)Q(s′,a′). The Expected SARSA target has the same expectation as the SARSA target; it just removes the variance that comes from "the next action is sampled at random".

(c) Q-learning converges to the optimal action values Q∗, regardless of how the behaviour policy explores. Conditions: tabular; every state–action pair visited infinitely often; the step sizes for each state–action pair satisfy ∑t​αt​=∞, ∑t​αt2​<∞; bounded rewards; γ<1 (Watkins and Dayan, 1992). A fixed step size α=0.5 fails the third condition and only jitters around Q∗.

SARSA learns the value of the policy it is executing. With ε fixed, under the same step-size and visitation conditions, it does not converge to Q∗, but to the fixed point of the "ε-greedy operator":

Q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γs′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[(1−ε)a′max​Q(s′,a′)+∣A∣ε​a′∑​Q(s′,a′)].

This operator is also a γ-contraction with a unique fixed point; it is the value of the best policy among all policies that "keep ε exploration". For SARSA to converge to Q∗, ε must gradually decrease to 0 while every action is still tried infinitely often (these conditions are called GLIE, greedy in the limit with infinite exploration; Singh et al., 2000).

An example you can compute: take the two-state MDP (γ=0.8; A: stay gives +1 and stays in A, go gives −1 and moves to B with 3/4; B: stay gives +5 and stays in B with 3/4, cash gives +7 and returns to A). Its Q∗ is (11.4, 13; 19, 17.4), and in both states the best and second-best actions differ by 1.6. Suppose the fixed point is Q∗−c; then each state's value under ε-greedy is V∗(s)−c−2ε​×1.6=V∗(s)−c−0.16, and substituting back gives c=0.8(c+0.16), c=0.64. So every Q value SARSA learns with ε=0.2 is 0.64 below Q∗, i.e. (10.76, 12.36; 18.36, 16.76). In this example the greedy actions don't change; in tasks where exploration is very costly, like "cliff walking", the two greedy policies differ too.

questions.q: No discounting (γ=1), only two non-terminal states A and B, and no actions to choose. Ten complete trajectories were collected, recorded as "state, reward, state, reward", with the end of the record meaning termination: 1 of A, 0, B, 0; 1 of A, 0, B, 1; 6 of B, 1; 2 of B, 0. This batch of data is replayed over and over until the value estimates stop changing (batch updating). (a) What V(A), V(B) does the Monte Carlo (MC) method give? (b) What does the temporal-difference method TD(0) give? (c) Why do the two V(A) values differ? In what sense is each one "optimal"? When should you trust which?
questions.a:
(a) Monte Carlo uses the average of the returns actually obtained after each state. B appears once in each of the 10 trajectories, and the returns after it are 0,1, six 1s and two 0s, for a total of seven 1s: V(B)=7/10=0.7. A appears twice, with returns after it of 0+0=0 and 0+1=1: V(A)=0.5.

(b) The TD(0) fixed point requires the average TD error at each state to be zero. B terminates immediately, so its target is just the reward, V(B)=0.7, the same as Monte Carlo. Both of A's transitions are "reward 0, go to B", so V(A)=0+V(B)=0.7.

(c) The two methods answer two different questions.

  • Batch Monte Carlo minimizes the squared error of the returns on the training data: the only returns seen after A are one 0 and one 1, whose average is 0.5.
  • Batch TD(0) gives the exact values under the "maximum-likelihood Markov model", called the certainty-equivalence estimate: from the data, estimate that A always goes to B with reward 0 and that B's expected reward is 0.7, then solve the equations in this model.

If the process really is Markov, TD's answer is more trustworthy: it uses all 10 visits to B to estimate what happens after A, while Monte Carlo uses only the 2 trajectories that start from A. If the state is not Markov (for example, B reached from A is actually different from B at the start of an episode), TD's model assumption is wrong, and Monte Carlo doesn't rely on that assumption. This conclusion assumes: tabular, the same batch of data replayed repeatedly, and a small enough step size.

questions.q: A chain: s1​→s2​→⋯→s10​→ terminal, with no actions to choose. The reward at each step is independently +1 with probability 1/2 and −1 with probability 1/2, with no discounting (γ=1), so every state's true value is 0. The current estimates are V(s1​)=0, V(s2​)=0.5. (a) What are the Monte Carlo target and the TD(0) target used to update V(s1​)? For each, find its expectation, bias, variance, and mean squared error relative to the true value 0. (b) The reward actually received at the first step is +1 and the step size is α=0.1; after one TD(0) update, what does V(s1​) become? (c) Summarize the bias–variance trade-off between these two targets. The TD target is biased — does that make tabular TD(0) converge to the wrong value?
questions.a:
(a) Denote the ten rewards by r1​,…,r10​, each with mean 0 and variance 1.

  • The Monte Carlo target is the full return G=r1​+⋯+r10​. Expectation 0, bias 0; the variance is the sum of ten independent terms, 10; mean squared error 10.
  • The TD(0) target is r1​+V(s2​)=r1​+0.5. Expectation 0.5, bias +0.5 (all of it from the error in V(s2​)); the variance is just the variance of one reward, 1; mean squared error 1+0.52=1.25.

(b) The TD error is δ=r1​+V(s2​)−V(s1​)=1+0.5−0=1.5, and V(s1​)←0+0.1×1.5=0.15.

(c) The Monte Carlo target is unbiased, but its variance grows with the number of remaining steps, because it adds in all the randomness that follows. The TD target contains only one step of randomness, so its variance is small; the price is that it is biased whenever the next state's estimate is inaccurate. In this example the TD target's mean squared error is 1.25 versus 10 for Monte Carlo, which is why TD usually learns faster. n-step returns and TD(λ) interpolate between the two.

The bias does not make tabular TD(0) converge to the wrong place. The bias here is a bias of "the current target", coming from V(s2​) not yet being accurate; as V(s2​) is updated toward its true value, the bias disappears with it. For a fixed policy, tabular, every state visited infinitely often, and step sizes satisfying ∑t​αt​=∞, ∑t​αt2​<∞, TD(0) converges with probability 1 to the true values (Jaakkola, Jordan and Singh, 1994; Tsitsiklis, 1994). With function approximation it's different: the fixed point of linear TD generally isn't the best approximation in the least-squares sense.

questions.q: A multi-armed bandit problem: two Bernoulli arms with success probabilities μ1​=0.6 and μ2​=0.4, unknown to the algorithm in advance. Use ε-greedy with fixed ε=0.1: at each step, with probability 1−ε pull the arm with the highest sample mean, and with probability ε pull one of the two arms uniformly at random. (a) Write down the definition of regret, and express it in terms of the number of times each arm is pulled. (b) Prove that the expected regret after T steps is at least 0.01T; what is the minimum at T=104? (c) How should you change ε so that regret grows only as logT? What assumption does that need?
questions.a:
(a) Regret is "the expected reward you would get by always pulling the best arm" minus "the expected reward the algorithm actually gets":

RT​=Tμ∗−E[t=1∑T​rt​]=i∑​Δi​ E[Ni​(T)],

where μ∗=maxi​μi​, Δi​=μ∗−μi​ is arm i's gap, and Ni​(T) is the number of times it is pulled in the first T steps. Here only arm 2 has a gap, Δ2​=0.2.

(b) At every step there is probability ε of exploring uniformly, and when exploring, arm 2 is pulled with probability 1/2. So no matter how accurate the estimates are, the probability of pulling arm 2 at each step is at least ε/2=0.05, E[N2​(T)]≥0.05T, and

RT​≥0.2×0.05×T=0.01T.

At T=104 it is at least 100. Regret grows linearly in T. This lower bound is also close to the actual value: once the estimates settle, the greedy steps all pull arm 1, and the expected regret per step is exactly 0.01. Simulation (pulling arm 1 when the two estimates are equal) gives about 102 at T=104 and about 202 at T=2×104; choosing randomly on ties adds about 5 more.

(c) Let ε decay over time, εt​∝1/t. Then the total number of exploration steps is ∑t​εt​≈clnT, and regret can be made O(logT). The form given by Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer (2002) is εt​=min(1, cK/(d2t)), where K is the number of arms; the assumption is 0<d≤mini​Δi​ and a large enough constant c, in which case the probability of pulling a suboptimal arm at step t is O(1/t). The cost is that you need to know a lower bound on the gap in advance: if c/d2 is too small, there isn't enough exploration, the algorithm may stay on the wrong arm for a long time, regret is no longer logarithmic, and over a practical number of steps it can be close to linear. If you don't want to depend on the gap, use UCB or Thompson sampling.

questions.q: A multi-armed bandit problem with all rewards in [0,1]. At each step the UCB1 algorithm pulls the arm with the largest index xˉi​+2lnn/ni​​, where n is the total number of pulls so far, ni​ is the number of times arm i has been pulled, and xˉi​ is its sample mean. Now n=100: arm 1 has been pulled 90 times with mean 0.60; arm 2 has been pulled 10 times with mean 0.40. (a) Compute the indices of the two arms. Which arm is pulled next? (b) Use Hoeffding's inequality to explain why the added term is 2lnn/ni​​. (c) At what rate does UCB1's expected regret (the expected reward lost compared with always pulling the best arm) grow with the total number of steps T? Write down the upper bound you remember, and evaluate it when the two arms' true means are 0.6 and 0.4 and T=104. (d) Can this growth rate be improved?
questions.a:
(a) ln100=4.605.

  • Arm 1: 0.60+2×4.605/90​=0.60+0.320=0.920;
  • Arm 2: 0.40+2×4.605/10​=0.40+0.960=1.360.

The next pull is arm 2. Its sample mean is low, but it has only been pulled 10 times, so its uncertainty is much larger.

(b) With rewards in [0,1] and independent pulls, Hoeffding's inequality gives bounds in both directions: P(xˉi​≤μi​−a)≤exp(−2ni​a2) and P(xˉi​≥μi​+a)≤exp(−2ni​a2). Taking a=2lnn/ni​​, both right-hand sides are exp(−4lnn)=n−4. The first says the probability that the index xˉi​+a is below the true value μi​ is at most n−4, so the index is an upper confidence bound on μi​; applied to the optimal arm, it means the optimal arm is almost never underestimated. The second says a suboptimal arm's sample mean is almost never overestimated by more than a. n−4 decays fast enough that the sum over all times and all possible ni​ is still finite, so the total loss from "the confidence interval failing" is a constant.

When both bounds hold, a suboptimal arm i's index is at most μi​+2a, and the optimal arm's index is at least μ∗. So as soon as 22lnn/ni​​<Δi​, i.e. ni​>8lnn/Δi2​, the suboptimal arm's index is guaranteed to be below the optimal arm's. So each suboptimal arm is pulled only about 8lnn/Δi2​ times. This is "optimism in the face of uncertainty": arms that haven't been tried enough get a high score, and arms that have been tried enough and still fall short are naturally dropped.

(c) It grows as lnT. Theorem 1 of Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer (2002): if rewards are in [0,1] and each arm's rewards are i.i.d., then for any number of steps n,

Rn​≤8i:Δi​>0∑​Δi​lnn​+(1+3π2​)j∑​Δj​.

Plugging in Δ=0.2, n=104: 8×9.210/0.2+4.290×0.2=368.4+0.9=369.3. That corresponds to arm 2 being pulled at most about 1842+4.3 times. The constants in this bound are loose: in simulation, UCB1's regret at 104 steps is only a little over 60. But the order is right: doubling T from 104 to 2×104 adds only about ten points to UCB1's regret, while ε-greedy with fixed ε=0.1 adds 100.

(d) The order can't be improved, but the constant can. The Lai and Robbins (1985) lower bound: for Bernoulli arms, any "uniformly good" algorithm (regret o(Ta) on every problem instance, for all a>0) satisfies

T→∞liminf​lnTE[Ni​(T)]​≥KL(μi​∥μ∗)1​.

Here KL(0.4∥0.6)=0.4ln0.60.4​+0.6ln0.40.6​=0.2ln1.5=0.0811, so regret is asymptotically at least 0.08110.2​lnT≈2.47lnT. For reference, at T=104, 2.47lnT≈22.7; this is an asymptotic result and can't be treated as a strict lower bound at a finite number of steps. The coefficient in UCB1's bound is 8/Δ=40, far from 2.47; KL-UCB and Thompson sampling achieve this optimal constant.

questions.q: Two Bernoulli arms with unknown success probabilities, both with prior Beta(1,1) (i.e. uniform). So far: arm 1 has been pulled 3 times with 2 successes; arm 2 has been pulled once with 0 successes. (a) Write down the posterior distribution and posterior mean of each arm. (b) How does Thompson sampling choose the next arm? What is the probability that it chooses arm 2? What about being greedy with respect to the posterior mean? (c) Suppose arm 2 is pulled at this step and succeeds; what does its posterior become? (d) In a sentence or two, explain why Thompson sampling balances exploration and exploitation.
questions.a:
(a) The Beta distribution is the conjugate prior for a Bernoulli likelihood: for Beta(a,b), each observed success adds 1 to a, each observed failure adds 1 to b, and the mean is a/(a+b).

  • Arm 1: 2 successes, 1 failure, posterior Beta(3,2), mean 3/5;
  • Arm 2: 0 successes, 1 failure, posterior Beta(1,2), mean 1/3.

(b) Thompson sampling draws one sample θ1​, θ2​ from each arm's posterior and pulls the arm with the larger sample. So the probability it chooses arm 2 is the posterior probability that θ2​>θ1​. The density of Beta(3,2) is 12x2(1−x); the density of Beta(1,2) is 2(1−y), so P(θ2​>x)=(1−x)2. Hence

P(θ2​>θ1​)=∫01​12x2(1−x)(1−x)2dx=12∫01​x2(1−x)3dx=12⋅6!2!3!​=51​.

Thompson sampling pulls arm 2 with probability 1/5. Being greedy with respect to the posterior mean always pulls arm 1 (3/5>1/3), so the probability of choosing arm 2 is 0.

(c) Arm 2 gains one success, and its posterior becomes Beta(2,2), with mean 1/2.

(d) The probability that Thompson sampling picks each arm equals the posterior probability that "this arm is the optimal arm" (probability matching). An arm with little data has a wide posterior and a good chance of drawing a large value, which gives exploration; as data accumulates, the posterior narrows, clearly worse arms are almost never chosen again, and exploration winds down automatically. It needs no exploration parameter to tune. For Bernoulli arms, its regret asymptotically achieves the Lai–Robbins lower bound (Kaufmann, Korda and Munos, 2012).

groups.title: Off-policy evaluation, function approximation and reward shaping

questions.q: A one-step problem: action L gives reward 1, action R gives reward 0. The data are generated by a behaviour policy μ that chooses L with probability 1/2 and R with probability 1/2; the policy we want to evaluate is a target policy π that chooses L with probability 0.9 and R with probability 0.1. We draw n independent samples (ai​,ri​) from μ, with importance weights ρi​=π(ai​)/μ(ai​). The ordinary importance sampling estimate is V^OIS​=n1​∑i​ρi​ri​, and the weighted importance sampling estimate is V^WIS​=∑i​ρi​ri​/∑i​ρi​. (a) What is the true value vπ​? What are the weights of the two actions? (b) For n=1, what are the expectation, variance and mean squared error of each estimate? What is the variance if you draw one sample directly from π? (c) For n=2, find the expectation and mean squared error of the weighted estimate, and compare with the ordinary estimate. (d) Summarize the general bias and variance properties of the two estimators, and the conditions importance sampling needs to be valid.
questions.a:
(a) vπ​=0.9×1+0.1×0=0.9. The weights are ρ(L)=0.9/0.5=1.8 and ρ(R)=0.1/0.5=0.2.

(b) n=1.

  • The ordinary estimate is ρr: 1.8 when L is drawn and 0 when R is drawn, each half the time. Expectation 0.9, unbiased; variance 21​×1.82−0.92=0.81; mean squared error 0.81.
  • The weighted estimate is ρr/ρ=r; the weight cancels: 1 with probability 1/2 and 0 with probability 1/2. Expectation 0.5, bias −0.4; variance 0.25; mean squared error 0.25+0.16=0.41. With a single sample, the weighted estimate's expectation is actually the behaviour policy's value vμ​.
  • Drawing one sample directly from π: the reward is a Bernoulli variable with success probability 0.9, variance 0.9×0.1=0.09. Ordinary importance sampling has 9 times that variance.

(c) n=2. Four equally likely cases:

The two actions Ordinary estimate Weighted estimate
L, L (1.8+1.8)/2=1.8 3.6/3.6=1
L, R or R, L 1.8/2=0.9 1.8/2.0=0.9
R, R 0 0/0.4=0

Weighted estimate: expectation (1+0.9+0.9+0)/4=0.7, bias −0.2; mean squared error (0.12+0+0+0.92)/4=0.205. Ordinary estimate: expectation 0.9, variance (which is also the mean squared error) (0.92+0+0+0.92)/4=0.405. With two samples, the weighted estimate's mean squared error is already only half that of the ordinary estimate. The gap widens further on: at n=10 the weighted estimate has expectation 0.882 and mean squared error 0.0068, while the ordinary estimate has variance 0.081.

(d) General properties.

  • Ordinary importance sampling is unbiased. Its variance is driven by the weights; when the weights are unbounded, the variance can be very large or even infinite.
  • Weighted importance sampling is biased; the bias goes to 0 as n grows, so it is consistent. It is a weighted average of observed returns and never leaves the range of the returns, so with bounded returns its variance is bounded, and in practice it is usually more stable.
  • Both need coverage: wherever π(a∣s)>0 we need μ(a∣s)>0; otherwise things the target policy would do never appear in the data and can't be estimated. You also need to know (or be able to estimate) the behaviour policy's probabilities.

In multi-step problems the weight is the product of per-step ratios, and the variance grows exponentially with the number of steps; this is derived in the last question on the RL for LLMs page.

questions.q: (a) Which three things appearing together make up the "deadly triad"? Does it mean "guaranteed to diverge"? (b) An example: two states share one parameter w in a linear approximation; state 1's estimate is w and state 2's estimate is 2w. All rewards are 0, so all true values are 0. Repeatedly apply semi-gradient TD(0) updates using only the single transition "state 1 → state 2, reward 0", with γ=0.9, α=0.1, w0​=1. Write down the update and compute w after 10 updates. For what values of γ does w diverge? (c) Switch to on-policy sampling: each episode first goes from state 1 to state 2, then from state 2 to the terminal state (reward 0, terminal value 0), and each of the two transitions is updated once, in order. What is w after 10 episodes? (d) What happens if you remove any one of the three? Give a non-divergent example for each.
questions.a:
(a) The three things are: function approximation (different states share parameters), bootstrapping (using your own estimates as targets, as in TD and Q-learning), and off-policy training (the state distribution used for updates is not the one the target policy itself generates). When all three appear together, learning can be unstable or even diverge — not that it necessarily diverges; DQN with experience replay and a target network has all three, and in practice it often trains fine.

(b) The gradient of state 1's estimate w with respect to the parameter is 1. Semi-gradient TD(0) differentiates only the current state's estimate and treats the target as a constant:

w←w+α[r+γ⋅2w−w]⋅1=w[1+α(2γ−1)].

Plugging in γ=0.9, α=0.1: each update multiplies by 1.08. After 10 updates w=1.0810=2.159, and it keeps growing, whereas the correct answer is w=0. Whenever 2γ−1>0, i.e. γ>1/2, it diverges for any α>0 (w stays put at γ=1/2 and converges to 0 for γ<1/2). Intuitively: when state 1's estimate is pulled up toward 2γw, the shared parameter makes state 2's estimate rise by twice as much, so the target can never be caught.

(c) The gradient of state 2's estimate 2w with respect to the parameter is 2; its transition leads to the terminal state, so its target is 0:

w←w+α[0+0−2w]⋅2=w(1−4α)=0.6w.

The two updates in one episode together multiply by 1.08×0.6=0.648. After 10 episodes w=0.64810=0.013, converging to the correct 0. With on-policy sampling, state 2's own update pulls its inflated estimate back down; in (b) it diverges because state 2's estimate is only ever used as a target and is never corrected by its own transition.

(d) Remove any one, and the other two can coexist:

  • No function approximation: tabular Q-learning is both off-policy and bootstrapping, and under the conditions given in Q5 it converges to Q∗.
  • Not off-policy: linear function approximation with on-policy TD(0) converges when states are sampled from the policy's stationary distribution, the features are linearly independent, and the step sizes satisfy ∑t​αt​=∞, ∑t​αt2​<∞; the error at the limit point is at most a constant multiple of the best linear approximation error, and that multiple grows as γ→1 (Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1997).
  • No bootstrapping: using Monte Carlo returns as regression targets (with importance weights when off-policy) is ordinary supervised learning, and stochastic gradient descent converges under the usual conditions, at the cost of high variance.

In practice you usually keep all three but weaken one of them: target networks weaken bootstrapping, multi-step returns reduce reliance on bootstrapping, and keeping the replay data distribution close to the current policy reduces how off-policy the training is.

questions.q: A two-state MDP with discount factor γ=0.8. State A: stay gives +1 and stays in A; go gives −1, moves to B with probability 3/4, and stays in A with probability 1/4. State B: stay gives +5, stays in B with probability 3/4, and returns to A with probability 1/4; cash gives +7 and always returns to A. The optimal policy is known to be "go in A, stay in B", with values (V(A),V(B))=(13,19) and optimal action values Q∗(A,stay)=11.4, Q∗(A,go)=13, Q∗(B,stay)=19, Q∗(B,cash)=17.4; another policy, "go in A, cash in B", has value (10,15). To make the agent learn to go to B faster, someone proposes two reward shaping schemes. Scheme 1: add an extra 4 every time the agent transitions from A to B, leaving other transitions unchanged. Scheme 2: use the potential function Φ(A)=0, Φ(B)=5, and add F(s,s′)=γΦ(s′)−Φ(s) on every transition from s to s′. (a) Write down the extra reward under scheme 2 for the four transitions A→A, A→B, B→A, B→B. (b) Prove that scheme 2 does not change which of any two policies is better, and write down the new optimal action values. (c) Under scheme 1, what does the optimal policy become? Measured with the original rewards, how much worse is it than the true optimal policy? (d) What is wrong with scheme 1?
questions.a:
(a) Plugging into F(s,s′)=0.8Φ(s′)−Φ(s):

  • A→A: 0.8×0−0=0;
  • A→B: 0.8×5−0=+4;
  • B→A: 0.8×0−5=−5;
  • B→B: 0.8×5−5=−1.

The reward for entering B is the same as in scheme 1, but leaving B "pays the potential back".

(b) Along any trajectory starting from s0​, the discounted sum of the extra rewards telescopes:

t≥0∑​γt[γΦ(st+1​)−Φ(st​)]=−Φ(s0​)+T→∞lim​γTΦ(sT​)=−Φ(s0​).

So for any policy π and any (s,a), the new action value is Q′π(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Φ(s). The amount subtracted depends only on the current state, not on the action or the policy, so the ranking of actions within a state doesn't change, which of any two policies is better doesn't change either, and the optimal policy stays the same. The new optimal action values:

  • A: stay 11.4−0=11.4, go 13−0=13;
  • B: stay 19−5=14, cash 17.4−5=12.4.

This is the result of Ng, Harada and Russell (1999). Conditions: Φ depends only on the state and is bounded; the γ in F is the MDP's discount factor; undiscounted episodic tasks also require the terminal state's potential to be 0. They also proved the converse: if the extra reward is not of this form, there is always some MDP in which it changes the optimal policy.

(c) Scheme 1 only changes the expected reward of choosing go in A: −1+43​×4=2. Under the new rewards, compare B's two choices when A chooses go (write VA​, VB​). In both cases VA​=2+0.8(0.25VA​+0.75VB​), i.e. 0.8VA​=2+0.6VB​.

  • B chooses stay: VB​=5+0.8(0.75VB​+0.25VA​), i.e. VB​=12.5+0.5VA​. Solving gives VA​=19, VB​=22.
  • B chooses cash: VB​=7+0.8VA​. Solving gives 0.32VA​=6.2, VA​=19.375, VB​=22.5.

The cash option is higher in both states. Check that it satisfies the optimality equation: with (19.375,22.5), B's stay is 5+0.8(0.75×22.5+0.25×19.375)=22.375<22.5, and A's stay is 1+0.8×19.375=16.5<19.375. So under scheme 1 the optimal policy becomes "go in A, cash in B".

Under the original rewards, this policy's value is (10,15), while the true optimum is (13,19): 3 less in A and 4 less in B.

(d) Scheme 1 pays a reward every time you enter B but deducts nothing when you leave, so the loop "enter B, immediately return to A, enter B again" can collect the reward over and over. What the agent learns is to farm this loop, not to stay in B. In the potential-based scheme, going around a loop and back to the original state makes the extra rewards cancel under discounting, so there is nothing to farm. If you add shaping rewards, write them in the form γΦ(s′)−Φ(s); the common advice is to make Φ close to a rough estimate of V∗.

import itertools
import math
from fractions import Fraction as F

import numpy as np

SEED = 0
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# ---- the two-state MDP of Q1, Q2, Q3, Q5 and Q13 ----
# states: 0 = A, 1 = B.   actions in A: 0 = stay, 1 = go.   actions in B: 0 = stay, 1 = cash.
GAMMA = 0.8
P = np.array([[[1.0, 0.0], [0.25, 0.75]],        # P[s, a, s']
              [[0.25, 0.75], [1.0, 0.0]]])
R = np.array([[1.0, -1.0], [5.0, 7.0]])          # R[s, a]
POLICIES = list(itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=2))


def solve_policy(policy):
    """V^pi from the linear system (I - gamma * P_pi) V = r_pi."""
    p_pi = np.array([P[s, policy[s]] for s in range(2)])
    r_pi = np.array([R[s, policy[s]] for s in range(2)])
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(2) - GAMMA * p_pi, r_pi)


def iterate_policy(policy, sweeps=300):
    """V^pi by applying the Bellman expectation backup again and again."""
    v = np.zeros(2)
    for _ in range(sweeps):
        v = np.array([R[s, policy[s]] + GAMMA * P[s, policy[s]] @ v for s in range(2)])
    return v


def rollout_value(policy, start, episodes=20000, horizon=80):
    """V^pi(start) by simulating the chain; 0.8**80 is about 2e-8, so cutting there costs nothing."""
    s = np.full(episodes, start)
    ret = np.zeros(episodes)
    discount = 1.0
    for _ in range(horizon):
        a = np.array(policy)[s]
        ret += discount * R[s, a]
        s = (rng.random(episodes) < P[s, a, 1]).astype(int)
        discount *= GAMMA
    return ret.mean()


def bellman_opt(v):
    return (R + GAMMA * P @ v).max(axis=1)


# ---- Q1: V^pi for pi = (go, cash) ----
PI = (1, 1)
assert np.allclose(solve_policy(PI), [10, 15])
assert np.allclose(iterate_policy(PI), [10, 15])
assert abs(rollout_value(PI, 0) - 10) < 0.15 and abs(rollout_value(PI, 1) - 15) < 0.15

# ---- Q2: one step of policy improvement, the optimal policy, the myopic policy ----
q_pi = R + GAMMA * P @ solve_policy(PI)
assert np.allclose(q_pi, [[9, 10], [16, 15]])
improved = tuple(int(a) for a in q_pi.argmax(axis=1))
assert improved == (1, 0)                                    # A: go, B: stay
values = {pol: solve_policy(pol) for pol in POLICIES}
assert np.allclose(values[(0, 0)], [5, 15]) and np.allclose(values[(0, 1)], [5, 11])
assert np.allclose(values[(1, 0)], [13, 19]) and np.allclose(values[(1, 1)], [10, 15])
for pol in POLICIES:                                         # (go, stay) beats every other policy in both states
    assert np.all(values[(1, 0)] >= values[pol] - 1e-12)
v_star = np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(300):                                         # second route: value iteration
    v_star = bellman_opt(v_star)
assert np.allclose(v_star, [13, 19])
q_star = R + GAMMA * P @ v_star
assert np.allclose(q_star, [[11.4, 13], [19, 17.4]])

# ---- Q3: contraction, and how many sweeps value iteration needs ----
for _ in range(2000):
    v, u = rng.normal(0, 10, 2), rng.normal(0, 10, 2)
    assert np.abs(bellman_opt(v) - bellman_opt(u)).max() <= GAMMA * np.abs(v - u).max() + 1e-12

def run_td(kind, steps=100000):
    """Tabular SARSA or Q-learning on the MDP, eps-greedy behaviour, step size n(s, a) ** -0.7."""
    q, visits = np.zeros((2, 2)), np.zeros((2, 2))
    u = rng.random((steps + 1, 3))

    def act(state, row):
        return int(q[state].argmax()) if row[0] >= eps else int(row[1] < 0.5)

    s = 0
    a = act(s, u[0])
    for t in range(steps):
        s2 = int(u[t, 2] < P[s, a, 1])
        a2 = act(s2, u[t + 1])
        bootstrap = q[s2, a2] if kind == "sarsa" else q[s2].max()
        visits[s, a] += 1
        q[s, a] += (R[s, a] + GAMMA * bootstrap - q[s, a]) / visits[s, a] ** 0.7
        s, a = s2, a2
    return q

def bad_pulls(algo, horizon, checkpoints, runs=400, eps=0.1):
    """Mean number of pulls of the worse arm at each checkpoint, over independent runs (vectorised)."""
    rows = np.arange(runs)
    pulls, wins = np.zeros((runs, 2)), np.zeros((runs, 2))
    out = {}
    for t in range(1, horizon + 1):
        if algo == "ucb1" and t <= 2:
            arm = np.full(runs, t - 1)                       # pull each arm once to start
        elif algo == "ucb1":
            arm = (wins / pulls + np.sqrt(2 * math.log(t - 1) / pulls)).argmax(axis=1)
        else:
            arm = (wins / np.maximum(pulls, 1)).argmax(axis=1)
            arm = np.where(rng.random(runs) < eps, rng.integers(0, 2, runs), arm)
        pulls[rows, arm] += 1
        wins[rows, arm] += rng.random(runs) < MU[arm]
        if t in checkpoints:
            out[t] = pulls[:, 1].mean()
    return out

RHO, REW = {"L": F(9, 5), "R": F(1, 5)}, {"L": 1, "R": 0}


def exact_is(n):
    """Exact mean and variance of both estimators: enumerate all 2^n equally likely action sequences."""
    ordinary, weighted = [], []
    for seq in itertools.product("LR", repeat=n):
        num = sum(RHO[a] * REW[a] for a in seq)
        ordinary.append(num / n)
        weighted.append(num / sum(RHO[a] for a in seq))
    mean = lambda xs: sum(xs) / len(xs)
    var = lambda xs: mean([x * x for x in xs]) - mean(xs) ** 2
    mse = lambda xs: mean([(x - F(9, 10)) ** 2 for x in xs])
    return mean(ordinary), var(ordinary), mean(weighted), mse(weighted)
